PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 38536/97) against [LOCATION] lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an [NRP] national, Mr [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATE_TIME].

The applicant was represented before the Court by Mr [PERSON], a lawyer practising in [LOCATION]. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador [PERSON], Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that civil proceedings concerning him lasted unreasonably long.

The application was transmitted to the Court on [DATE_TIME], when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11).

The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court.

By a decision of [DATE_TIME] the Court declared the application partly admissible.

As of [DATE_TIME] the application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court.

THE FACTS

The applicant was a shareholder in a limited liability company, but assigned his shares to another shareholder in [DATE_TIME]. Subsequently, the company went bankrupt.

On [DATE_TIME] a bank which had extended credit to the company filed an action against the applicant with the Innsbruck Regional Court (Landesgericht) requesting repayment because of his joint and several liability for the credit.

On [DATE_TIME] the first hearing was held and on [DATE_TIME] the second. On [DATE_TIME] the file was transmitted to the Lienz District Court ([PERSON]) to hear two witnesses and the applicant. On [DATE_TIME] the Lienz District Court returned the file to the Innsbruck District Court. On [DATE_TIME] the file was transmitted to the Salzburg District Court to hear witnesses. The file was returned on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] was set down as date for the next hearing. It was postponed upon the applicant’s request and was eventually held on [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the court appointed a banking expert. On [DATE_TIME] the file was again transmitted to the Lienz District Court for the hearing of a further witness. It was returned on [DATE_TIME] and sent to the expert on [DATE_TIME]. The expert delivered his opinion on [DATE_TIME]. The applicant’s request for an extension of the time‑limit to comment on the expert opinion was granted and the time‑limit set at [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] another hearing was held.

On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court granted the bank’s claim having regard to the submissions of the parties, witnesses and the expert, to documentary evidence and to the case files of the bankruptcy proceedings.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant appealed against this decision. On [DATE_TIME] the Innsbruck Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) quashed the decision and referred the case back to the Regional Court.

A hearing which was scheduled by the Innsbruck Regional Court for [DATE_TIME] had to be postponed as the claimant had failed to submit necessary documents and a witness could not be summoned. It was held on [DATE_TIME]. Subsequently, the applicant requested legal aid and on [DATE_TIME] requested an extension by [DATE_TIME] of the time-limit for submitting his declaration of means. On [DATE_TIME], after the applicant had been granted legal aid, the expert was ordered to supplement his opinion. The expert complied with this order on [DATE_TIME]. After a hearing was held on [DATE_TIME], the expert was again ordered to supplement his opinion. On [DATE_TIME] the expert informed the court that both parties had failed to submit documents required. On [DATE_TIME] a further hearing was held at which the court dismissed the applicant’s motion for bias concerning the expert. The next hearing was held on [DATE_TIME] and on [DATE_TIME] the file was again transmitted to the expert. On [DATE_TIME] the expert submitted his supplemented opinion. On [DATE_TIME] a further hearing was held.

On [DATE_TIME] the Innsbruck Regional Court again granted the bank’s claim. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant appealed against the decision.

On [DATE_TIME] the Innsbruck Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal.

On [DATE_TIME] the Supreme Court ([PERSON]) dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The decision was served on [DATE_TIME].

name: Tommy Evaldsson
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 75252/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the levying of monitoring fees on the individual applicants’ wages involved violations of Articles 9, [DATE_TIME], and 14. The Court declared the application admissible with respect to the five individual applicants and inadmissible insofar it concerned the Swedish Construction Industries (Sveriges Byggindustrier) (hereinafter “the Industries”) The case was heard in public in [LOCATION] (Rule 59 § 3). The relevant local branch of the Union in the instant case was the [LOCATION] branch, Byggettan. If inspections were carried out in accordance with the collective agreement, the local branch had the right to reimbursement of the costs involved on the basis of a fee of 1.5% of the worker’s wages. In a subsequent dispute between the Industries and the Union over the interpretation of the accord, an out-of-court settlement was reached on [DATE_TIME] to the effect that it applied to all workers belonging to a trade union other than the Union. The applicants requested to be exempt from the deductions. The case concerned fees for monitoring the wages for [DATE_TIME] work. The company complied with their requests, stopped paying the fees to Byggettan and did not provide it with the above-mentioned wage information concerning the applicants. The Union disagreed with the Industries, arguing that the monitoring fees could not be seen as tantamount to forced membership of the Union. The system of monitoring fees did not involve a compulsion to join a trade union. Moreover, the applicants had not expressed any ideological reasons for their unwillingness to contribute to the monitoring work. They submitted that they opposed the deductions because they did not think the work was of any use to them and considered the deductions an unnecessary expense. Industrialists argued that a ban on the levying of monitoring fees on unorganised workers’ wages would violate the positive rights of its members. The Labour Court rejected the Industries’ claims. The court found no reason to determine whether the monitoring fees generated a surplus which contributed to other union activities. The inspection of time-based wages aimed at securing the observance of the collective labour agreement and also served as a basis for the statistics used by the Union in wage negotiations with the employers. Consequently, the monitoring benefited the general union activities and the fees contributed financially to those activities. In the instant case the applicants were not subjected to pressure to leave their organisation. Instead, the question was to what extent they were protected by a right to negative freedom of association. The Labour Court initially concluded that the monitoring fee deductions did not entail membership of the Union. It found that no pressure had been exerted to compel the applicants to join the Union against their will. The court found that there was no indication that they opposed the deduction of the fees because they took exception to union activities in general or to the ideology of the union. The Labour Court noted that, theoretically, the applicants could be inclined to join a trade union other than the Union in order to avoid the wage deduction for the monitoring fees. But it found, however, that it was not very realistic that an employee would regard the wage deductions as a particular incentive to do so. Court concluded that all the above considerations indicated that the deductions did not breach the applicants’ rights under the Convention. As the fee was not tantamount to forced membership of the Union and had not influenced or forced the applicants to join the Union, the company had been obliged to make a deduction from their wages in accordance with the collective labour agreement. Court could not find that the monitoring fee was intended as a measure to pressure them to joining the Union – the court could not finds that it had any such coercive effect. The court concluded that the deduction was in line with the Collective Labour Agreement and was not a breach of the applicants' rights.

The case originated in an application (no. 75252/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 75252/01) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by five [NRP] nationals, Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON] (“the applicants”), and the Swedish Construction Industries (Sveriges Byggindustrier) (hereinafter “the Industries”) on [DATE_TIME].

The applicants alleged that the levying of monitoring fees on the individual applicants’ wages involved violations of Articles 9, [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME] and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

By a decision of [DATE_TIME], the Court declared the application admissible with respect to the five individual applicants and inadmissible insofar it concerned the Industries.

A hearing took place in public in [LOCATION], [LOCATION], on [DATE_TIME] (Rule 59 § 3). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr [PERSON], Ministry for Foreign Affairs, Agent, [PERSON], Ministry of Industry, Employment and Communications, Mr [PERSON], Ministry for Foreign Affairs, [PERSON], Ministry of Industry, Employment and Communications, Advisers; (b) for the applicants Mr [PERSON], Representative, Counsel, Mr [PERSON], Representative, Co-counsel, Mr [PERSON], Lawyer, Mr [PERSON], Head of the Lawyers’ Section of the Industries, [PERSON], Lawyer, Advisers, Mr [PERSON], Applicant. The Court heard addresses by Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON].

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicants were born in [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] respectively. They were employed by the construction company LK Mässinteriör AB (hereinafter “the company”) [DATE_TIME] [DATE_TIME] on a time-wage basis.

The company, being a member of the Industries, was bound by a collective labour agreement, the Construction Agreement (Byggnads-avtalet), concluded between the Swedish Building Workers’ Union ([PERSON], hereinafter “the Union”) and the Industries. The relevant local branch of the Union in the instant case was the [LOCATION] branch, Byggettan.

At the material time, eight employees in the company carried out work covered by the labour agreement. Three of these workers were members of the Union whereas the five applicants were not members of the Union or of any other trade union.

Under section 3, subsection f 5 of the collective agreement, as it stood at the relevant time, the local branch had the right to inspect on a continuous basis wage conditions by measuring piecework (ackordsarbete) and result work ([PERSON]), as well as monitoring time-based work (tidlönearbete). If inspections were carried out in accordance with the collective agreement, the local branch had the right to reimbursement of the costs involved on the basis of a fee of 1.5% of the worker’s wages. The employer was obliged to deduct this amount from the worker’s wages and to supply the local branch with the information necessary for the inspection work.

On [DATE_TIME] the Industries and the Union concluded an accord pursuant to which a worker organised in a trade union other than the Union could request his or her employer not to deduct the inspection fee, with the result that the Union would no longer have the right to request either information or the payment of a fee in respect of that worker. In a subsequent dispute between the Industries and the Union over the interpretation of the accord, an out-of-court settlement was reached on [DATE_TIME] to the effect that it applied to all workers belonging to a trade union other than the Union.

On [DATE_TIME] the company and Byggettan concluded an agreement concerning the inspection work. The agreement gave details of the work and specified, inter alia, that it was the company’s responsibility to provide Byggettan with the wage information and to deduct fees from the wages of the workers and pay them to Byggettan six times a year. The information was to include the place of work, the names and social security numbers of the workers and [DATE_TIME] and net wages.

The applicants requested to be exempt from the deductions, which in their case concerned fees for monitoring the wages for [DATE_TIME] work. The company complied with their requests, stopped paying the fees to Byggettan and did not provide it with the above-mentioned wage information concerning the applicants. Byggettan insisted on payment and initiated formal local negotiations. These were held on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME]. However, no solution was reached, either in the local negotiations or in the subsequent central negotiations between the Industries and the Union.

The Industries eventually brought the case before the Labour Court (Arbetsdomstolen), seeking a declaratory judgment to the effect that the company was not obliged to levy the monitoring fees in question. It argued that the inspection of wages, in so far as it did not concern the technical measuring of piecework, aimed at securing the observance of the provisions of the collective labour agreement and was therefore part of the general activities of the Union. Moreover, the [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] [DATE_TIME] reports of Byggettan allegedly showed that the inspection fees greatly exceeded the costs of the work and that the surplus was used for general union activities. Consequently, the corresponding deductions from the applicants’ wages were tantamount to forced union membership or, at least, involved an unacceptable compulsion to join the Union or another trade union. The conduct thus violated their negative freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention as well as under domestic law. Furthermore, since the applicants did not share the political values of the Union, the levy on their wages also violated their rights under Article 10 of the Convention.

Two of the applicants, Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON], were heard by the Labour Court. They submitted that they opposed the deductions because they did not think that the monitoring work was of any use to them and considered the deductions an unnecessary expense. Allegedly, they also submitted that they felt that the deductions were unjust.

The Union disagreed with the Industries, arguing that the monitoring fees could not be seen as tantamount to forced membership of the Union, such membership being secured through the payment of a separate membership fee. The system of monitoring fees did not involve a compulsion to join a trade union. Moreover, the applicants had not expressed any ideological reasons for their unwillingness to contribute to the monitoring work. The Union claimed that, contrary to the Industries’ allegation, the [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] [DATE_TIME] reports of Byggettan showed that the proceeds of that work had not contributed to general union activities but that, in fact, the monitoring had been run at a loss. Furthermore, the inspection work was strictly separated, economically and otherwise, from the other activities of Byggettan. Finally, arguing that the positive aspect of the freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention was stronger than its negative counterpart, the Union claimed that a ban on the levying of monitoring fees on unorganised workers’ wages would violate the positive rights of its members, as this could induce members to leave the Union in order to avoid paying the fees.

By a judgment of [DATE_TIME], the Labour Court rejected the Industries’ claims. It referred to several of its previous judgments concerning various types of measurement and monitoring fees. In a case from [DATE_TIME] ([DATE_TIME] nr 222), the court had found that the monitoring of time-based wages was wholly different from the measuring of piecework, as no special action had to be taken to establish the amount and type of work performed. Instead, the inspection of time-based wages rather aimed at securing the observance of the collective labour agreement and also served as a basis for the statistics used by the Union in wage negotiations with the employers. Consequently, the monitoring benefited the general union activities and the fees contributed financially to those activities. The court had therefore concluded that the levying of fees on the wages of members of the Syndicalist Union for monitoring work carried out by another trade union involved a violation of those worker’s positive freedom of association, as they would have to resign from their own organisation in order to avoid contributing to both organisations. The Labour Court stated that there was no reason to come to a different conclusion in the instant case as to the nature of the monitoring work. Thus, from the point of view of association law, there was no reason to distinguish between monitoring work and general union activities. Having reached that conclusion, the court found no reason to determine whether the monitoring fees generated a surplus which contributed to other union activities. However, the situation in the instant case was different from the [DATE_TIME] case in that the applicants were not subjected to pressure to leave their organisation. Instead, the question was to what extent they were protected by a right to negative freedom of association. The Labour Court noted that the negative freedom of association under domestic law was exclusively based on the Convention. It referred to the European Court’s case-law and drew the conclusion that only the core of the negative freedom of association was protected under Article 11 of the Convention, meaning that a person must have been subjected to a certain measure of force or at least strong pressure to join an organisation in order to give rise to a violation of Article 11. The Labour Court initially concluded that the monitoring fee deductions did not entail membership of the Union and that no pressure had been exerted to compel the applicants to join the Union against their will. It further found that the fact that the applicants, through payment of the monitoring fee, indirectly supported the activities of the Union did not in itself amount to forced membership, since being a member of the Union also entailed certain other duties, such as loyalty to its objectives and payment of a membership fee. The situation would have been different if the applicants would to some extent have been associated with the Union’s ideology as a result of the monitoring fee deductions. However, the fee in issue was deducted in accordance with their employer’s obligations under the collective labour agreement, and it was, accordingly, difficult to see a link with the Union’s ideology. In this connection, the court also referred to the evidence given before it by Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON]. While it questioned whether the grounds for their position in the case could have a bearing on their negative freedom of association, the court nevertheless found that there was no indication that they opposed the deduction of the fees because they took exception to union activities in general or to the ideology of the Union. The Labour Court went on to state that, while the applicants, through the fee deductions, contributed to the general activities of the Union, they were not treated any differently from Union members as concerns the monitoring. In order to monitor the observance of the collective labour agreement, the work was carried out with respect to all employees affected by the agreement, whether belonging to a trade union or not. Noting that it could appear offensive to an unorganised worker to have to contribute to the work, the court stated that it was not without importance that the unorganised worker in fact obtained something in return for the fee paid. The Labour Court further noted that, theoretically, the applicants could be inclined to join a trade union other than the Union in order to avoid the wage deduction for the monitoring fee. It found, however, that it was not very realistic that an employee would regard the wage deduction as a particular incentive to do so. The Labour Court concluded that all the above considerations indicated that the deductions did not breach the applicants’ rights under the Convention. As to the main issue to be determined – whether the monitoring fee was intended as a measure to pressure them to join the Union – the court could not find that it had any such coercive effect. As the fee was not tantamount to forced membership of the Union and had not influenced or forced the applicants to join the Union, the company had been obliged to make a deduction from their wages in accordance with the collective labour agreement.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant in his lustration declaration stated that he had not collaborated, served or worked for the communist-era security services. On [DATE_TIME] he informed the Speaker of the Sejm that he had had contacts with the military counter-intelligence.

On an unspecified date the Commissioner of Public Interest ([PERSON]) informed the applicant that he had doubts as to the truthfulness of his lustration declaration and invited him for an interview on [DATE_TIME]. At the next interview the applicant was invited to read the records concerning his alleged collaboration.

On [DATE_TIME] the Commissioner applied to the Warsaw Court of Appeal to institute lustration proceedings against the applicant on the grounds that he had lied in his lustration declaration by denying that he had collaborated with the secret services.

On [DATE_TIME] the Warsaw Court of Appeal decided to allow the Commissioner’s request and instituted lustration proceedings against the applicant.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant’s lawyers consulted the classified part of the case file in the secret registry of the court. On both occasions the lawyers were entitled to take notes in the special notebook kept by the Head of the secret registry. However, they did not avail themselves of that possibility.

On [DATE_TIME] the Warsaw Court of Appeal, acting as the first‑instance lustration court, found that [DATE_TIME] the applicant had been an intentional and secret collaborator of the military counter-intelligence service and had therefore submitted an untrue lustration declaration. One judge from the panel of three expressed a dissenting opinion. The judgment was served on the Commissioner of Public Interest, the applicant and his lawyer.

The applicant lodged an appeal in which he maintained, in particular, that as a member of the armed forces he had been ordered to collaborate with the military counter-intelligence agency and that, therefore, his collaboration did not fall within the ambit of the Lustration Act. Alternatively, he argued that when submitting his declaration he had made a justifiable error. According to the Government, the applicant’s appeal did not concern the issue of restrictions on access to the case file.

On [DATE_TIME] the Katowice Court of Appeal, acting as the second‑instance lustration court, upheld the impugned judgment.

The applicant lodged a cassation appeal against the judgment. The Government submitted that the applicant had not invoked the issue of restrictions on access to the case file in his cassation appeal.

On [DATE_TIME] the Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal as manifestly ill-founded. The decision was served on the applicant on [DATE_TIME].

The applicant is prevented from standing in elections and from holding other public functions for a period of [DATE_TIME].

According to the Government, in the course of the proceedings before the Katowice Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court neither the applicant nor his lawyer availed themselves of the possibility to consult the case file or to take notes of it.

test_texts:
PROCEDURE

The present case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission“) on [DATE_TIME], within the [DATE_TIME] period laid down by Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. The case originated in an application (no. 9248/81) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Commission on [DATE_TIME] under Article 25 (art. 25) by a [NRP] citizen, Mr. [PERSON].

The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and [DATE_TIME] (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby [LOCATION] recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed violations by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, [DATE_TIME] and 13 (art. 8, art. 10, art. 13) of the Convention.

In response to the inquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30).

The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. [PERSON], the elected judge of [NRP] nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr. [PERSON], the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 3 (b)). On [DATE_TIME], the President drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the five other members, namely Mr. [PERSON], Mr. [PERSON], Mr. L.-E. [PERSON], Sir [PERSON] and Mr. [PERSON] (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 4) (art. 43). Mr. [PERSON], substitute judge, subsequently replaced Mr. [PERSON], whose term of office as judge had expired before the hearing, and at a later stage Mr. [PERSON] and Mr. [PERSON], substitute judges, replaced Mr. [PERSON] and Mr. [PERSON], who were prevented from taking part in the consideration of the case (Rules 2 § 3, 22 § 1 and 24 § 1).

Mr. [PERSON] assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 § 5). He ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Swedish Government (“the Government“), the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant regarding the need for a written procedure (Rule 37 § 1). On [DATE_TIME], he directed that the lawyer and, should he so decide, the Agent should each have until [DATE_TIME] to file a memorial and that the Delegate should be entitled to reply in writing within [DATE_TIME] from the date of the transmission to him by the Registrar of whichever of the aforesaid documents should last be filed. The applicant’s memorial was received at the registry on [DATE_TIME]. By letter [DATE_TIME], the Agent of the Government stated that the Government did not intend to file any memorial. On [DATE_TIME], the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegate would present his observations at the hearing.

On [DATE_TIME], after consulting, through the Registrar, the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant, the President directed that the oral proceedings should open on [DATE_TIME] (Rule 38). On [DATE_TIME], the Commission communicated to the Registrar a number of documents whose production he had requested on the instructions of the President. On [DATE_TIME], certain additional documents furnished by the applicant were received at the registry.

The hearing was held in public at [LOCATION], [LOCATION], on the appointed day. Immediately before it opened, the Court had held a preparatory meeting. There appeared before the Court:

for the Government Mr. [PERSON], Ambassador, Under-Secretary for Legal and Consular Affairs, Ministry for Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr. [PERSON], Assistant Under-Secretary, Ministry of Justice, Mr. [PERSON], Head of Division, National Police Board, Advisers;

for the Commission Mr. [PERSON], Delegate;

for the applicant Mr. [PERSON], Counsel, Mr. [PERSON], Adviser.

The Court heard addresses by Mr. [PERSON] for the Government, by Mr. [PERSON] for the Commission and by Mr. [PERSON] for the applicant, as well as their replies to questions put by the Court and several judges.

AS TO THE FACTS

I. PARTICULAR CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant, Mr. [PERSON], is a [NRP] citizen born in [DATE_TIME] and a carpenter by profession.

On [DATE_TIME], he started to work as a temporary replacement in a post of museum technician (vikarierande museitekniker) at the Naval Museum at [LOCATION] in the south of [LOCATION]. The museum is adjacent to [LOCATION] which is a restricted military security zone. The applicant maintained before the Court that the intention was that he should work for [DATE_TIME] in this post, while its ordinary holder was on leave. He alleged that on [DATE_TIME] he was told to leave his work pending the outcome of a personnel control which had to be carried out on him in accordance with the Personnel Control Ordinance [DATE_TIME] (personal-kontrollkungörelsen 1969:446 - see paragraphs 18-34 below). According to the applicant, this control had been requested on [DATE_TIME]. The Government submitted that the applicant was employed only from [DATE_TIME], as evidenced by a notice to this effect, issued on [DATE_TIME] by the Director of the Museum. They further contended that in employing Mr. [PERSON] the Director had committed two mistakes. Firstly, it was not in accordance with the procedure prescribed in the Ordinance and the relevant regulations issued thereunder to employ a person before a personnel control had been undertaken and, secondly, the post had not been properly declared vacant.

The necessary steps were taken on [DATE_TIME]. The post was opened for application until [DATE_TIME]. Mr. [PERSON] did not apply.

It appears that on [DATE_TIME] the Director informed him that the outcome of the personnel control had been unfavourable and that he could therefore not be employed at the Museum.

Following the advice of the Security Chief of [LOCATION], the applicant wrote to the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy (chefen för marinen) requesting to be informed of the reasons why he could not be employed at the Naval Museum. In his reply of [DATE_TIME], the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy stated, inter alia: “The Museum possesses several storage rooms and historical objects within the area for the security of which the Chief of [LOCATION] ([LOCATION]) is responsible. According to the information received by the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy, the person holding the post in question must have freedom to circulate within areas subject to special restrictions regarding access. The rules on access to these areas must therefore also be applied to the personnel employed at the Museum. It is for these reasons that the Chief of the Naval Base requested a personnel control. The control carried out has provided such grounds for the Commander-in-Chief’s assessment of you from a security point of view that the decision has been taken not to accept you. However, if your duties at the Naval Museum will not necessitate that you have access to the naval installations at [LOCATION], the Commander-in-Chief sees no reason to oppose your employment. The decision whether or not to employ you is taken in a procedure distinct from the present one.“

On [DATE_TIME], the applicant complained to the Government and requested that the assessment of the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy be cancelled and that he be declared acceptable for the temporary employment at the Naval Museum, irrespective of the possibility of being reinstated in that employment. He pointed out in particular that he had left a permanent position in [LOCATION], in [LOCATION], on being told that he was accepted for employment at the Naval Museum and that a negative outcome of the personnel control could mean social misery, especially considering that he had a wife and child to support. In his original complaint, and also in a letter of [DATE_TIME], Mr. [PERSON] further requested that he be given information about the reasons for his not being accepted at the Naval Museum. The Government requested the opinion of the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces (överbefälhavaren), who in turn consulted the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy. The Commander-in-Chief of the Navy explained in a letter of [DATE_TIME] that he had received the result of the personnel control from the Supreme Commander on [DATE_TIME] together with the following proposal: “Accepted in accordance with the assessment of the [Commander-in-Chief of the Navy], on condition that [PERSON] does not, through access to the Museum’s premises or through his work, obtain insight into secret activities.“ The Commander-in-Chief of the Navy added that, according to his information, the Director of the Museum required the person employed in the post in question to have free access to, and freedom to circulate in, [LOCATION] and that accordingly, on [DATE_TIME], he had taken the decision not to accept the applicant. In his reply to the Government, the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces stated, inter alia: “However, the employment of Mr. [PERSON] during this time, 15 [DATE_TIME], did not involve any access to [LOCATION]. The Commander-in-Chief of the Navy has said that he does not oppose such employment. The Director of the Naval Museum has, however, affirmed the requirement that Mr. [PERSON] should have access to [LOCATION]. In view of the above and the fact that, if Mr. [PERSON] was given access to [LOCATION], he would have access to secret installations and information, the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy decided not to accept the applicant. When dealing with the present case, the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy has entirely followed existing regulations concerning the assessment of personal qualifications from a security point of view. ... Like the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy, the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces considers that Mr. [PERSON] may properly be employed by the Naval Museum provided that the holder of the appointment does not require access to [LOCATION].“ The opinion of the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces was accompanied by a secret annex, containing the information on Mr. [PERSON] released by the National Police Board (rikspolisstyrelsen). This annex was never communicated to the applicant and has not been included in the material submitted to the Court.

In a letter of [DATE_TIME], the applicant raised new grievances before the Government. These concerned the decision of the National Police Board not to exercise its powers under section 13 of the Personnel Control Ordinance to communicate to him the information released on him (see paragraph 31 below). The applicant requested that the Government should, before taking a decision on his request of [DATE_TIME], give him the right to be apprised of and to comment upon the information thus released by the Board. On this matter, the Government sought the opinion of the Board. In its reply of [DATE_TIME], the Board proposed that the applicant’s complaints be dismissed. It added: “The entering of information in the register of the Board’s Security Department is based mainly on a [DATE_TIME] Royal Decree which is secret. Before information is entered, the question of registration is subject to assessment, at several levels, by civil servants under responsibility to verify compliance with the above-mentioned rules in relation to each item of information. In the event of doubt, the question of registration is decided upon by the Chief of the Security Department. Information from the register is handed out in accordance with section 9 of the Personnel Control Ordinance after decision by the National Police Board in plenary meeting. At least three of the six members of the Board who are appointed amongst parliamentarians should be present when decisions are taken in matters of personnel control. In the case of the applicant, all six members were present. ... Under section 13 of the Personnel Control Ordinance, the person whom the information concerns ought to be given the opportunity to submit observations on the matter if special reasons give cause for this. However, the National Police Board did not see any cause to apply this provision in the case of the applicant as no special reasons were found, and also as the registering had been effected in accordance with the secret Royal Decree and disclosure of the information would have revealed part of the contents of that Decree.“ Mr. [PERSON] replied to this opinion in a letter of [DATE_TIME] to the Government, in which he argued, inter alia, that the Board should have communicated to him, at least orally and subject to a duty of confidentiality, the information kept on him.

By decision of [DATE_TIME], the Government rejected the whole of the applicant’s complaint. In its operative parts, the decision read: “The question whether or not a person is suitable for certain employment can only be examined by the Government in the context of a complaint about the appointment to a post. [PERSON] has lodged no appeal with the Government in respect of appointment. His request that the Government should declare him acceptable for the provisional employment concerned cannot therefore be examined. In the present case, there are no such special circumstances as are mentioned in section 13 of the Personnel Control Ordinance which would give [PERSON] the right to be acquainted with the information about him released by the National Police Board to the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces. The remainder of [PERSON]’s petition is a request to be given an extract from, or information about the contents of, a police register. The Government reject [this] request ... The Government do not examine [PERSON]’s request for a revised assessment of his person and take no measure in regard to any other part of his petition.“

The applicant maintained before the Court that he still did not know the content of the secret information recorded on him. In a judgment of [DATE_TIME] the Colmar Court of Appeal upheld that order for the following reasons: “Under Article 388 of the Customs Code the court may make an express order for a person who has been convicted of a [customs] offence or offence relating to indirect taxation to remain in custody, even if an ordinary appeal or appeal on points of law has been lodged, until he or she has paid the fiscal penalties imposed on him or her. The courts have consistently held that customs law is a special branch of law and an exception to the general law. In the present case, the express reference in the Customs Code to the Code of Criminal Procedure relates only to the length of the imprisonment in default. Consequently, since the Criminal Court made an express order – upheld by the Court of Appeal – under Article 388 of the Customs Code for enforcement of the order for imprisonment on the ground of anticipatory default, the provisions of Articles 749 et seq. of the Code of Criminal Procedure giving the President of the tribunal de grande instance jurisdiction to hear urgent applications are inapplicable.”

On [DATE_TIME] the Court of Cassation ruled that the applicant's appeal on points of law against that decision had lapsed, as he had not lodged written pleadings in support of his appeal within the statutory time-limit.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant made an application for an order for the prison sentence and the term of imprisonment in default to run concurrently, arguing that he was serving two prison sentences for the same offence.

He alleged a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention, which sets out the non bis in idem rule, and of Article 6 of the Convention. He relied in particular on the Court's judgment in [PERSON] v. [LOCATION] (judgment of [DATE_TIME], Series A no. 317-B), in which imprisonment in default was found to constitute a “penalty” for the purposes of the Convention.

In a judgment of [DATE_TIME] the Colmar Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's application on the grounds that, firstly, “the European Court of Human Rights' judgments are declaratory and therefore not binding on the trial court, which is only required to apply the European Convention on Human Rights”; and, secondly, “imprisonment in default possesses the legal characteristics not of a penalty, but of a means of enforcement attached to the financial penalties whose recovery they are intended to secure”. The Court of Appeal concluded from that that Article 5 of the former Criminal Code, which required sentences to run concurrently, had not been infringed by the trial court and could not enable a prison sentence and term of imprisonment in default to be served concurrently.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation against that judgment. In a judgment of [DATE_TIME] the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal for the following reasons: “The appellant cannot validly argue that, by sitting in private in accordance with Article 711 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Court of Appeal infringed Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights ... The requirement for a public hearing laid down by that provision applies only to proceedings for 'the determination of a criminal charge' and cannot therefore be relied on with respect to proceedings relating, as in the instance case, to an application for a ruling that sentences be served concurrently ... The impugned judgment and procedural documents show that the appellant, [PERSON], was found guilty of an offence under the drug-trafficking and customs-offences legislation and, inter alia, sentenced to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment and a customs fine. After being ordered to serve [DATE_TIME] imprisonment in default of payment, he made an application for a ruling that that term should run concurrently with the prison sentence. In dismissing that application, the Court of Appeal found, in particular, that imprisonment in default possesses the legal characteristics not of a penalty, but of a means of enforcement attached to the financial penalties whose recovery they are intended to secure. In these circumstances, the Court of Appeal has justified its decision and the alleged grievance is without foundation ...”

The applicant, who has now completed all the sentences he was required to serve, was deported to [LOCATION], where he came from, pursuant to the permanent exclusion order.

PROCEDURE

The case originated in two applications (nos. 29612/05 and 30668/05) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two [NRP] nationals, Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON] (“the applicants”), on [DATE_TIME].

The applicants were represented by [PERSON], a lawyer practising in [LOCATION]. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent.

On [DATE_TIME] the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time (Article 29 § 1).

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicants were born in [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] respectively.

On [DATE_TIME] a large group of demonstrators, including the applicants, gathered in [LOCATION] in front of the Galatasaray High School in [LOCATION] to attend the reading out of a statement to the press in protest against the NATO summit which was being held in [LOCATION] on [DATE_TIME]. The demonstration was organised by [PERSON] (Kamu Emekçileri [PERSON] – The Confederation of Public Employees’ Trade Unions). A large group of police officers, all wearing helmets and gas masks and equipped with the necessary material, was also deployed to the area. Nearly 500 demonstrators took part in the demonstration and slogans were chanted against NATO. After the statement was read out by the representative of [PERSON], the demonstrators started to disperse. A small group of demonstrators, carrying the flags of their non-governmental organisation [PERSON] (Peoples’ Houses), walked towards the police officers who had blocked [LOCATION] to prevent the group from approaching [LOCATION]. The demonstrators attacked the police officers with sticks and stones and the police officers used tear gas and truncheons to disperse the group. Some of the nearby shops and vehicles were damaged during the incident. According to the incident report, six police officers were wounded during the incident.

The applicants, who had listened to the press statement, were arrested during this incident. According to the applicants, they were beaten and insulted during and after their arrest. [DATE_TIME], they were taken to the Bayrampaşa Health Clinic for a medical examination. According to the applicants, the doctor examined them in the presence of the police officers. A copy of the medical report is not included in the case file.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicants were taken to the Beyoğlu Forensic Medicine Institute for a further medical examination. The doctor who examined the applicants concluded that both of them were unfit to work for [DATE_TIME]. The following findings were noted in the medical report: – [PERSON]: Large bruises on the back of the upper left arm, bruises on the back, bruises on the shoulders and on the waist, bruises on the right shoulder, bruises on the left gluteal region, tenderness of the left leg. – [PERSON]: Several bruises on the back of the left shoulder, bruise on the upper side of the right shoulder blade, bruises on the left and right sides of the back, a bleeding wound on the left elbow, a bruise on the right knee, bruises on the left knee. The doctor also noted that the applicant had a nose bleed.

[DATE_TIME], the applicants were released upon the order of the Beyoğlu Public Prosecutor.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicants filed a petition with the [PERSON] public prosecutor against the police officers who had carried out their arrest. In their petition, the applicants complained, inter alia, that their arrest had been unlawful and that the police officers had used excessive force during and after the arrest.

On [DATE_TIME] the [PERSON] public prosecutor issued a decision of non-prosecution in respect of the police officers who had been on duty at the relevant time. In his decision, the public prosecutor considered that the force used by the security forces had been in line with Article 16 of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police and had not been excessive. In the public prosecutor’s opinion, the injuries sustained by the applicants had been caused by a use of force which was proportionate. In delivering this decision, the public prosecutor had regard to the fact that after the press statement had been read out, a group of seventy people had not dispersed and had attacked the police officers with sticks and stones, also causing damage to nearby shops and vehicles. In the public prosecutor’s opinion, the force used by the police had therefore been proportionate.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicants filed an objection against the public prosecutor’s decision.

On [DATE_TIME] the Istanbul Assize Court dismissed the applicants’ objection.

In the meantime, on [DATE_TIME], the [PERSON] public prosecutor filed a bill of indictment against eighteen accused, including the applicants, with the Beyoğlu Criminal Court and accused them under Article 32 of Law no. 2911 of taking part in an illegal demonstration without prior authorisation and of not dispersing despite the police officers’ warning. The court accordingly stated that there was no evidence in the file to support a finding that the applicants had violated Law no. 2911 or resisted the police officers as alleged.

name: Johangir Abbas Butt
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47017/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their deportation from [LOCATION] to [LOCation] would entail a violation of their rights under Article 8. The Norwegian Government (“the Government”) were represented by Mr [PERSON], Attorney at the Office of the Attorney General (Civil Affairs), as their Agent. The application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicants and their mother had lived in [LOCATION]. The authorities observed that the applicants had strong attachment to [ LOCATION] since they had lived and gone to school in that country. The Directorate of Immigration decided to withdraw the applicants’ and their mothers’ settlement permit, on the ground that the permit had been granted on the basis of false information provided by the mother. The Ministry of Justice upheld the Directorate’s decision. Several successive requests for reconsideration were rejected. In [DATE_TIME] the children were apprehended with a view to being deported to [LOCation]. However, the police decided not to do so, based on their information that they had no contact with the mother or with the family in [ LOCation]. The police considered that it would be inappropriate to expel them without their mother. The applicants lodged a previous application (no. 565/08) under the Convention, complaining that their deportation to [LOCATION] would constitute a violation of Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention. The Immigration Appeals Board, in two separate decisions, rejected the applicants’ requests for modification of the decision of [DATE_TIME] revoking their settlement (and residence) permit and, as regards the second applicant, the Board’s decision to expel him indefinitely. The applicants did not pursue their application. The proceedings giving rise to the present application are outlined in the next section of this article. The application is being dealt with by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) on behalf of the applicants. The applicants challenged the Immigration Appeals Board’s decision of [DATE_TIME]. In this connection they both requested an interlocutory injunction to stop their deportation. Both requests were rejected by the City Court and the High Court. The City Court observed that the applicants had lived in [LOCATION] during major parts of their childhood and that they had relatively strong attachment to their home country. The Oslo City Court quashed the decision of the immigration Appeals Board, disagreeing with the Board's assessment that they lacked special attachment to [ LOCATION]. The High Court rejected both requests for an injunction. The second applicant was ordered to leave the country indefinitely. The applicants had not had contact with their father since [DATE_TIME] and did not wish to have any contact with him. Their mother had died and it was uncertain whether they had other relatives in the country. They were able to speak [PERSON] and to understand the language in oral form but could not read or write it. The applicants had gone to school in [LOCATION], had friends and acquaintances there and were mastering the [NRP] language, both oral and written. The City Court considered that they had special ties to [ LOCATION]. Accordingly, the Immigration Appeals Board’s decisions of [Date_TIME) were to be quashed. The State appealed to the Borgarting High Court, which overturned the City Court’s ruling by a judgment of [DATE_TIME] The High Court found it clear that the refusal to grant residence permits constituted an interference with the applicants’ rights under paragraph 1 of Article 8 of the Convention. In considering whether the interference was justified under paragraph 2, the central question was whether the measure was “necessary in a democratic society”. The High court found it hardly probable that the applicants had no contacts with their mother and had no knowledge of her whereabouts. The authorities’ omission to implement ‘the refusal of residence’ (“oppholdsnektelsen”) ought to be seen in the light of ECHR 2006‑I. The applicants had not possessed [NRP] passports and the police had done nothing to arrange for them to obtain such passports. The applicants could reasonably perceive the authorities to mean that they were not expected to travel to [LOCATION] on their own. It was difficult to ascribe any responsibility to the applicants for not having taken any steps to leave the country while the mother had gone into hiding from the police. After reaching the age of majority, the applicants’ choice to stay in [ LOCATION] had been something for which they ought to bear the risk and responsibility. They had developed a strong personal and social attachment to [location]. They had received the essential part of their education and upbringing. The High Court, nonetheless, with doubt, arrived at the conclusion that the refusal of residence had not been unlawful as being contrary to Article 8 of the Convention. It attached decisive weight to the fact that the applicants’ strong attachment to [LOCATION] had been established during unlawful residence. It also noted that they as adults had relatively good possibilities for settling in [ LOCATION]. The special circumstances pointed to above regarding the background to the applicants were also discussed. The High Court’s view, the applicants still had certain links to their country of origin, though they might encounter social and professional difficulties upon return. The applicants had stated that they were unable to write in [PERSON] and were speaking a ‘childish’ Urdu. They both mastered English well, which was an official language in [LOCation]. The Supreme Court refused the applicants leave to appeal. The Immigration Appeals Board decided to stay the implementation of the applicants’ deportation to [LOCATION]. The police dropped the charges concerning threats on [DATE_TIME]. No further information has been submitted in respect of these criminal proceedings. According to the applicants during [Date_TIME] they took refuge in [ LOCATION], [LOCation]. The Supreme Court ruled that the applicants were entitled to stay in Sweden. The Appeals Leave Committee of the Supreme Court found that such leave was not warranted by the importance of the decision for other cases or by other considerations. The decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal.

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 47017/09) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two [NRP] nationals, [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON] (“the applicants”), on [DATE_TIME].

The applicants were represented by Mr [PERSON], a lawyer practising in [LOCATION]. The Norwegian Government (“the Government”) were represented by Mr [PERSON], Attorney at the Office of the Attorney General (Civil Affairs), as their Agent.

The applicants alleged that their deportation from [LOCATION] to [LOCATION] would entail a violation of their rights under Article 8 of the Convention.

On [DATE_TIME] the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1).

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The first and second applicants, who are sister and brother, were born in [LOCATION] in [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] respectively and live in [LOCATION].

A. Factual background to the present application

In [DATE_TIME] the applicants arrived in [LOCATION] with their mother and were in view of the children’s particular situation granted a residence permit on [DATE_TIME] on the ground of strong humanitarian considerations (section 8(2) of the former [DATE_TIME] Immigration Act, see paragraph 45 below).

During [DATE_TIME] the mother returned with the children to [LOCATION], where the children first lived with their grandparents and then with their father and his wife. There they stayed until the turn of the year 1995‑1996, when the mother resettled in [LOCATION] with the children. In the meantime, on [DATE_TIME] the Directorate of Immigration had granted them a settlement permit, while being ignorant about their stay in [LOCATION] from [DATE_TIME].

In [DATE_TIME] the applicants’ father applied for family reunification. His application, which was refused, prompted an investigation by the immigration authorities which revealed that for most of the period from [DATE_TIME] to [DATE_TIME] the applicants and their mother had lived in [LOCATION]. The authorities further observed that the applicants had strong attachment to [LOCATION] since they had lived and gone to school in that country from [DATE_TIME] to [DATE_TIME] and because their father still lived there. On [DATE_TIME] the Directorate of Immigration decided to withdraw the applicants’ and their mothers’ settlement permit, on the ground that the permit had been granted on the basis of false information provided by the mother about her and the children’s residence in [LOCATION]. It was also decided to refuse them further residence in [LOCATION].

On [DATE_TIME] the Ministry of Justice upheld the Directorate’s decision. Several successive requests for reconsideration were rejected. In [DATE_TIME] the children were apprehended with a view to being deported to [LOCATION]. However, the police decided not to do so, based on their information that they had no contact with the mother or with the family in [LOCATION]. The police considered that it would be inappropriate to expel them without their mother who had disappeared around the turn of [DATE_TIME]. The applicants had no contacts with their mother until she was hospitalised in [LOCATION] in [DATE_TIME]. During this period they lived with an uncle and aunt in [LOCATION].

On [DATE_TIME] the second applicant was convicted for unprovoked aggravated physical assault, having hit another person with his fist causing a fracture to the victim’s nose and a two centimetres scar on his eyelid that had to be stitched. For this and certain other offences (withdrawal of 4,600 [NRP] Krone (NOK) from cash points by using another person’s credit card; driving a stolen moped and the possession of 0.2 gram of hashish) he was sentenced to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment.

In the light of these offences, the Immigration Appeals Board decided on [DATE_TIME] to expel him indefinitely, with reference to section [DATE_TIME]) of the [DATE_TIME] Immigration Act, as he had been convicted for an offence that was punishable by [DATE_TIME] imprisonment.

In [DATE_TIME] the applicants sought to challenge the validity of the decision of [DATE_TIME] and, as regards the second applicant, that of [DATE_TIME]. By a judgment of [DATE_TIME] the Oslo City Court upheld their action.

In [DATE_TIME] the mother was expelled to [LOCATION], in compliance with the immigration authorities’ decision (see paragraph 8 above). She died in [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the Borgarting High Court found against the applicants. It was observed that when the settlement permit was revoked in [DATE_TIME], the applicants had in reality resided unlawfully in [LOCATION] for [DATE_TIME]. At that time they had close relatives in [LOCATION], including their father, with whom they had lived for periods [DATE_TIME]. Nor did the High Court find that the decision of [DATE_TIME] regarding the second applicant was disproportionate.

On [DATE_TIME] the Appeals Leave Committee of the Supreme Court refused the applicants leave to appeal.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicants lodged a previous application (no. 565/08) under the Convention, complaining that their deportation to [LOCATION] would constitute a violation of Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention. They also requested an interim measure to stay their deportation under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court. On [DATE_TIME] the request was refused. The applicants did not pursue their application. On [DATE_TIME], a Committee of three judges decided to strike it out of the Court’s list of cases (Article 37 § 1 of the Convention).

B. The proceedings giving rise to the present application

1. The Immigration Appeals Board’s decisions of [DATE_TIME]

In the meantime, on [DATE_TIME] the Immigration Appeals Board, in two separate decisions, rejected the applicants’ requests for modification of the decision of [DATE_TIME] revoking their settlement (and residence) permit and, as regards the second applicant, the Board’s decision of [DATE_TIME] to expel him indefinitely from [LOCATION]. The Board observed that such modification was not warranted either by strong humanitarian considerations or a strong attachment to [LOCATION] (section 8 (2) of the former [DATE_TIME] Immigration Act).

As regards the first applicant the Board had regard to the fact that she had not had a residence permit since [DATE_TIME] and that any links established after this date ought to carry little weight. Furthermore, all of the first applicant’s closest family lived in [LOCATION] and her brother, the second applicant, had been ordered to leave [LOCATION] indefinitely.

As regards the second applicant the Board quoted from its decision of [DATE_TIME] and maintained its previous view: “As to the [second applicant’s] attachment to [LOCATION], the Board has attached particular weight to the fact that during the period from [DATE_TIME] to [DATE_TIME], when he had a residence permit in [LOCATION], he had essentially lived in [LOCATION]. By the Ministry of Justice’s decision of [DATE_TIME] his settlement permit was finally revoked. He does not have a residence permit and is obliged to leave the country. In practice, links that are established during unlawful residence carry little weight. Reference is also made to the fact that [the second applicant’s] mother and sister do not hold a residence permit and are obliged to leave the country. In addition, the applicant has close family in his home country. He therefore ought to be seen as having relatively strong attachment to his home country. The Board cannot see that the [second applicant’s] current situation has been significantly changed since the situation considered in the decision of [DATE_TIME].”

In respect of both applicants the Board also referred to the reasoning and conclusions in earlier decisions and judgments and emphasised that its conclusions in the present decisions ought to be viewed in the context of those.

2. Judicial appeals against the Board’s decision of [DATE_TIME]

In [DATE_TIME] the applicants challenged that decision before the courts. In this connection they both requested an interlocutory injunction to stop their deportation. These requests were rejected by the City Court on [DATE_TIME] and the High Court on [DATE_TIME]. (a) The City Court

By a judgment of [DATE_TIME], the Oslo City Court quashed the Immigration Appeals Board’s decision of [DATE_TIME], disagreeing with the Board’s assessment that the applicants lacked special attachment to [LOCATION].

The City Court observed that the applicants, respectively twenty-one and [DATE_TIME], had lived in [LOCATION] for [DATE_TIME] during major parts of their childhood and the entirety of their adolescence. The question was what weight should be attached to their residence in [LOCATION] since they had been obliged to leave the country in [DATE_TIME].

It had not been possible for the applicants to obtain the necessary travel documents before they reached the age of majority in [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME], respectively. In such a situation the unlawful character of their sojourn had to be disregarded. There was little reason to emphasise their mother’s lack of cooperation in leaving the country. Nor could the applicants be said to have escaped implementation of the deportation, either before [DATE_TIME] or thereafter, as it had been decided on [DATE_TIME] not to implement the deportation. With the exception of [DATE_TIME], no active steps had been taken to implement the decision to expel the applicants and no attempts had been made to this effect pending the judicial proceedings, until [DATE_TIME]. Therefore, the applicants’ residence in [LOCATION] since [DATE_TIME] ought to carry a not insignificant weight in the assessment of whether they had special attachment to [LOCATION].

The City Court further observed that in [LOCATION] the applicants had close relatives – uncles and aunts – and had lived with these since [DATE_TIME]. The applicants had gone to school in [LOCATION], had friends and acquaintances there and were mastering the [NRP] language, both oral and written. Whilst the Immigration Appeals Board had found that the applicants had relatively strong links to [LOCATION], the City Court found that these had almost ceased. They had not had contact with their father since [DATE_TIME] and did not wish to have any contact with him. Their mother had died and it was uncertain whether they had other relatives in the country. They were able to speak [PERSON] and to understand the language in oral form but could not read or write it.

In view of the applicants’ longstanding residence in and attachment to [LOCATION] and their little or no connection to [LOCATION], the City Court considered that they had special ties to [LOCATION]. Accordingly, the Immigration Appeals Board’s decisions of [DATE_TIME] were to be quashed. In making a new assessment the Board ought to take as a premise that the applicants had strong attachment to [LOCATION] and that it was empowered under the Immigration Act to grant them a residence permit. (b) The High Court

The State appealed to the Borgarting High Court, which overturned the City Court’s ruling by a judgment of [DATE_TIME] and upheld the Immigration Appeals Board’s refusal of [DATE_TIME] as being lawful.

The High Court found it clear that the refusal to grant residence permits constituted an interference with the applicants’ rights under paragraph 1 of Article 8 of the Convention. In considering whether the interference was justified under paragraph 2, the central question was whether the measure was “necessary in a democratic society”. The High Court had regard to the consideration that where family life has been created at a time when the persons involved were aware that the immigration status of one of them was such that the persistence of that family life within the host State would from the outset be precarious the removal of the non-national family member would be incompatible with Article 8 only in exceptional circumstances ([PERSON] and [PERSON] v. the [LOCATION], no. 50435/99, §§ 38 and [DATE_TIME], ECHR 2006‑I) and [PERSON] and Others v. [LOCATION], no. 265/07, [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME]).

In balancing the competing interests the High Court considered it important when the applicants had become aware that their sojourn in [LOCATION] was unauthorised. It was clear that at the latest when they had been apprehended in [DATE_TIME] they had understood that they did not possess a residence permit. Their explanation that they had been unaware until then of their residence status was reliable. At that time they had been [DATE_TIME], respectively.

The applicants had further stated that their mother had gone under ground at around the turn of [DATE_TIME], and that she had stayed in hiding until [DATE_TIME], without theirs having any contact with her or being aware of her whereabouts. However, in [DATE_TIME] the police had found her handbag with her passport at her brother’s home. The High Court found it hardly probable that the applicants had no contacts with their mother and had no knowledge of her whereabouts from [DATE_TIME] until [DATE_TIME]. The authorities’ omission to implement “the refusal of residence” (“oppholdsnektelsen”) ought to be seen in the light of the fact that the police had been unable to get hold of their mother.

Nonetheless, there was reason to assume that during [DATE_TIME] the police did not in practice expect the applicants to leave the country on their own and that they would not be deported without their mother. In any event, the applicants could reasonably perceive the situation in this manner. Shortly after their arrest in [DATE_TIME] the applicants had been released because their mother could not be found and it was deemed unfortunate to deport them without her. It had further been clear that the applicants had not possessed [NRP] passports and that the police had done nothing to arrange for them to obtain such passports. Until passing the age of majority in [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME], respectively, the applicants had been dependent on the assistance of the [NRP] authorities to obtain passports.

The reason why the applicants had not been deported together with their mother when she was expelled on [DATE_TIME] was that the main hearing in the applicants’ case had been scheduled for [DATE_TIME] and that the immigration authorities had found it correct to give them the opportunity to attend the hearing.

Since the applicants could reasonably perceive the authorities to mean that they were not expected to travel to [LOCATION] on their own, it was difficult to ascribe any responsibility to the applicants for not having taken any steps to leave the country while the mother had gone into hiding from the police. However, after reaching the age of majority, the applicants’ choice to stay in [LOCATION] had been something for which they ought to bear the risk and responsibility.

There were generally speaking strong immigration policy considerations in favour of identifying children with the conduct of their parents. If it were to be otherwise, there would be a great risk that parents exploited the situation of their children to secure a residence permit for themselves and for the children. However, in the present case there had been no such risk as the applicants had reached the age of majority and their mother was dead.

The applicants had developed a strong personal and social attachment to [LOCATION]. They had received the essential part of their education and upbringing there, they mastered the language to the full and their education had been adapted to the [NRP] job market. The applicants had until [DATE_TIME] lived with their uncle and aunt (their mother’s brother and sister) with family in [LOCATION]. They were therefore presumed to have close emotional links to this part of the family. This was also where they had their friends and social network. The first applicant had completed high school and education as a lawyer’s secretary and was currently working in a media monitoring bureau. The second applicant had been pursuing high school as a private candidate.

As regards the applicants’ links to [LOCATION], these had since their mother’s death in [DATE_TIME] and foremost related to their father. They had not seen him after they had returned to [LOCATION] in [DATE_TIME] at [DATE_TIME], respectively. An uncle (a brother of their late mother) living in the same area of [LOCATION] as the father had met the applicants when visiting his siblings in [LOCATION] [DATE_TIME]. Moreover, the deceased mother had left a house in a well-off area of [LOCATION], in the vicinity of where the uncle lived. The father occupied parts of the house and let out the remainder. According to [NRP] inheritance rules, the applicants and the father were entitled to [DATE_TIME], respectively, of the house. Moreover, the applicants had stated that they were unable to write in [PERSON] and were speaking a “childish” Urdu. They both mastered English well, which was an official language in [LOCATION]. Thus, in the High Court’s view, the applicants still had certain links to their country of origin, though they might encounter social and professional difficulties upon return.

It also observed that in the experience of the Immigration Appeals Board, it was rare that one was confronted with cases where the duration of the unlawful stay had been nearly as long as in the present case. One could therefore question whether general immigration policy considerations, which normally carried weight in cases of unlawful residence, would be sufficiently weighty to regard the refusal of residence as being “necessary in a democratic society”.

The High Court, nonetheless, with doubt, arrived at the conclusion that the refusal of residence had not been unlawful as being contrary to Article 8 of the Convention. It attached decisive weight to the fact that the applicants’ strong attachment to [LOCATION] had been established during unlawful residence, that they still had links to their home place in [LOCATION] and that they as adults had relatively good possibilities for settling in [LOCATION]. The special circumstances pointed to above regarding the background to the applicants’ continuing residence in [LOCATION] for [DATE_TIME] could not be regarded as “exceptional circumstances” in the sense that this criterion had been applied by the European Court in its case-law. No new circumstances had occurred between the two decisions of [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] (see paragraphs 11 and 17 above) that could warrant a different conclusion than that reached by the High Court in its judgment of [DATE_TIME] (see paragraph 14 above). (c) The Supreme Court

On [DATE_TIME] the Appeals Leave Committee of the Supreme Court refused the applicants leave to appeal finding that such leave was not warranted by the importance of the decision for other cases or by other considerations. (d) Other developments

On [DATE_TIME] an article published by the newspaper Dagbladet, which included an interview with the applicants, stated that they lived at an undisclosed address.

On [DATE_TIME] the police arrested the applicants at an apartment in [LOCATION], belonging to their maternal uncle and aunt in [LOCATION]. The City Court ordered the applicants’ detention for a period of [DATE_TIME]. Before the City Court the first applicant said that she had all the time lived at the apartment of her maternal uncle in [LOCATION]. She had occasionally gone to the flat in Y Street where her aunt lived in order to fetch things. According to information contained in the City Court’s order of the same date to detain the second applicant for [DATE_TIME], he had first cohabited with a girlfriend in a studio outside [LOCATION] from [DATE_TIME]. Before and after, he had lived at his uncle and aunt’s apartment in [LOCATION].

During his ensuing detention, the police sought to have him detained on account of a separate matter, namely on suspicion of threats committed against his girlfriend. An indictment was issued on [DATE_TIME]. The second applicant denied the accusations in the main. The police dropped the charges concerning threats on [DATE_TIME]. No further information has been submitted in respect of these criminal proceedings.

According to the applicants during [DATE_TIME] they took refuge in [LOCATION], [LOCATION].

On [DATE_TIME] the Immigration Appeals Board decided to stay the implementation of the applicants’ deportation to [LOCATION].
